title: Record a Redis message in unacked in the step that pops it
body:
Fixes #305.

This is the wake list option from [my plan on the issue](https://github.com/celery/kombu/issues/305#issuecomment-6723857758), on by default. A Redis consumer now writes each message to `unacked` in the same step that takes it off its queue. On main, `BRPOP` takes the message and a second command records it, so a worker killed between the two loses the message, even with `task_acks_late` and `task_reject_on_worker_lost`.

- A Lua script pops from the first non-empty list and writes `unacked` in the same step, like the transport's `REFRESH_BINDING` script. The record is the one `QoS.append` writes, byte for byte, so workers on either version ack and restore each other's messages. `basic_get` uses the script too. With `no_ack`, nothing is recorded.
- A consumer whose queues are empty waits with `BLPOP` on a wake list per queue. Publishing, batch publishing and restoring a message push a token to that list, which keeps at most one. Deleting or purging the queue removes the list, and it expires with a queue that has `x-expires`.

Upgrade publishers first. A consumer of this version still gets messages from an older publisher, but only when its wait times out, after up to `brpop_timeout` (1 second by default). The docs say this in a `versionchanged:: 5.7.1` note, for the issue's 5.7.x milestone.

Most of the diff is tests: the transport changes by +350/−43 lines and the docs by +26, and the tests add about 1,370. What they show:

- A Hypothesis state machine shows that no message is lost or duplicated across publishes, pops, kills (also mid-pop), credit changes, acks, rejects and restores, also once the visibility timeout passes. It fails on main.
- A property shows that the script writes exactly what `QoS.append` writes, so old and new workers ack and restore each other's messages.
- The kill, `SIGSTOP` and `noeviction` tests reproduce the failures seen in practice, and fail on main.
- Guard tests show that nothing else changed, from delivery order and leftover keys to an idle consumer's commands, older publishers and a burst on idle consumers.

I'd like review on three things: whether the amount of tests suits kombu, the publisher change with its upgrade-publishers-first note, and the Redis CPU cost for large messages (about twice main's at 100 KB).

With a prefork worker killed with `SIGKILL` every 0.8 to 1.6 seconds while countdown tasks keep arriving:

| | Tasks lost | Runs that lost a task |
| --- | --- | --- |
| main | 9 of 3,200, 41 kills | 4 of 4 |
| This PR | 0 of 3,200, 40 kills | 0 of 4 |

The cost against main is in the folded comparison below: Redis CPU per message grows with message size, and each publish pushes a token.

<details>
<summary>Kill reproduction setup</summary>

Celery `768e476`, kombu main `445027e`, Redis 7.4.12. `-P prefork -c 4`, `task_acks_late`, `task_reject_on_worker_lost`, `visibility_timeout=60`, a task every 20 ms with a countdown of 1 to 8 s. The worker is killed with `SIGKILL` every 0.8 to 1.6 s and started again. Task ids are logged before each publish, and a fresh worker drains the queue and `unacked` at the end. Runs of main and this PR were interleaved, 800 tasks per run. No worker ever received a task that main lost. After the commits that keep callbacks from blocking on a Redis reply, 2 more runs each: main lost 4 of 1,600 tasks over 20 kills, and this PR none of 1,600 over 23 kills. After the put back of a reply without credit, 2 more: main lost 3 of 1,600 over 21 kills, and this PR none of 1,600 over 22 kills.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Cost against main and the plain wake list from the plan</summary>

One consumer (`drain_events`, prefetch 4, ack in the callback) and one publisher, on a Redis 7.4.12 container used by nothing else. Median of 3 interleaved runs, 200 byte messages unless noted. Commands are counted by Redis (`INFO commandstats`, which counts commands run inside a script), round trips by the client. "Plain wake list" is the code from the plan.

| Per message unless noted | main | Plain wake list | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Publish: Redis commands / round trips | 2 / 2 | 6 / 2 | 4 / 2 |
| Publish: Redis CPU / publisher CPU | 0.062 / 0.33 ms | 0.075 / 0.39 ms | 0.073 / 0.38 ms |
| Batch publish: Redis commands / round trips | 2 / 1.0 | 4 / 1.0 | 4 / 1.0 |
| 5,000 queued: messages per second | 1,180 | 1,708 | 1,569 |
| 5,000 queued: commands / consumer round trips | 9 / 3 | 9 / 2 | 10 / 2 |
| 5,000 queued: Redis CPU / consumer CPU | 0.112 / 0.51 ms | 0.104 / 0.33 ms | 0.119 / 0.37 ms |
| 5,000 queued: bytes sent to Redis | 1,068 | 373 | 373 |
| 500 queued 100 KB messages: Redis CPU | 0.34 ms | 1.04 ms | 0.67 ms |
| Idle consumer, a message every 20 ms: latency p50 / p99 | 2.4 / 3.9 ms | 2.2 / 4.3 ms | 2.2 / 3.7 ms |
| Same: commands / consumer round trips | 11 / 3 | 25 / 4 | 14 / 3 |
| Same: Redis CPU, publisher included | 0.44 ms | 0.58 ms | 0.51 ms |
| Same with 100 KB messages: Redis CPU | 0.67 ms | 1.61 ms | 1.18 ms |
| Same from a publisher without this change: latency p50 / p99 | | | 527 / 1,073 ms |
| No messages: commands per second, 1 queue / 3 queues | 1.4 / 1.4 | 6.4 / 14.4 | 5.9 / 13.1 |
| No messages: round trips / Redis CPU per second | 1.3 / 3.0 ms | 2.3 / 3.1 ms | 2.2 / 3.2 ms |

The publish counts include the routing lookup (`SMEMBERS`) that every publish to a named exchange makes. Each publish now also pushes the token and trims the list, in the same round trip.

Against the plain wake list, this PR decodes only the properties (Redis CPU for a 100 KB message 1.04 to 0.67 ms), has the script report an empty queue so the consumer waits instead of popping again (25 to 14 commands and 4 to 3 round trips for each message to an idle consumer), and publishes without `MULTI`/`EXEC` (6 to 4 commands). I also tried checking the queues with `EXISTS` before popping: idle commands went from 5.9 to 3.2 per second, but every pop paid for one more command and Redis CPU didn't change, so I left it out.

A Celery worker (`-P prefork -c 4`, Celery `768e476`) on 20,000 queued tasks, then a task every 20 ms, then 60 s idle. Median of 3 interleaved runs with `task_acks_late`, one run with the default early ack. CPU is read from `/proc` in 10 ms ticks.

| | main | Plain wake list | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tasks per second, acks late / early | 638 / 667 | 943 / 869 | 957 / 783 |
| Worker main process CPU per queued task, acks late / early | 1.18 / 1.14 ms | 0.87 / 0.92 ms | 0.86 / 1.02 ms |
| Pool processes CPU per queued task | 0.48 ms | 0.47 ms | 0.46 ms |
| Worker main process CPU per task, a task every 20 ms | 1.57 ms | 1.57 ms | 1.47 ms |
| Worker main process CPU per idle second | 0.83 ms | 1.0 ms | 1.17 ms |
| `apply_async()` CPU per task | 0.45 ms | 0.54 ms | 0.52 ms |
| RSS of the main process / pool processes, start and end | 62 / 230, 63 / 236 MB | the same | the same |

A large message takes about twice the Redis CPU of main: Redis copies a message into Lua and back at about 1.4 µs per KB, and the record copies it again. `apply_async()` takes about 0.07 ms more, for the pipeline that pushes the token with the message. The idle worker's extra 0.3 ms per second is about two 10 ms ticks over the 60 s, at the edge of what this measures.

Callbacks and latency with a message every 20 ms to an idle consumer, measured with the event loop (`Hub`) and with `drain_events()`, on the final head, `d2eb6f6` (before the put back) and main. The tables above were measured at `216b3e0`, before the change that keeps callbacks from blocking on a Redis reply. Median of 3 interleaved runs of 300 messages; a p99 of 300 is the third longest, so it moves between runs. Both paths take 3 round trips per message on all three.

| | main | `d2eb6f6` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Event loop: callback p50 / p99 / longest | 1.28 / 2.61 / 5.1 ms | 0.42 / 1.17 / 1.6 ms | 0.35 / 1.10 / 1.3 ms |
| Event loop: latency p50 / p99 | 1.64 / 3.6 ms | 1.51 / 3.6 ms | 1.46 / 2.5 ms |
| Same with `polling_interval=1` | 1.60 / 3.0 ms | 1.56 / 3.5 ms | 1.52 / 3.9 ms |
| `drain_events()`: latency p50 / p99 | 1.61 / 4.4 ms | 1.53 / 3.2 ms | 1.40 / 5.5 ms |
| Same with `polling_interval=1` | 1.64 / 5.5 ms | 1.53 / 3.7 ms | 1.44 / 4.9 ms |

On main a callback does more work per message, since it also sends the record. Here a message takes two callbacks, the wake-up and the pop, and neither blocks on a Redis reply. At `216b3e0`, a consumer with `polling_interval=1` slept after each stale token, for a median latency of 513 ms.

The same cost bench on the final head, `d2eb6f6` and main (median of 3 interleaved runs, a separate run from the table above):

| Per message unless noted | main | `d2eb6f6` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5,000 queued: messages per second | 1,406 | 1,760 | 1,931 |
| 5,000 queued: commands / consumer round trips | 9 / 3 | 10 / 2 | 10 / 2 |
| 5,000 queued: Redis CPU / consumer CPU | 0.094 / 0.45 ms | 0.106 / 0.33 ms | 0.097 / 0.31 ms |
| Idle consumer: latency p50 / p99 | 1.96 / 3.1 ms | 1.93 / 2.8 ms | 1.92 / 3.4 ms |
| Same: commands / Redis CPU, publisher included | 11 / 0.37 ms | 14 / 0.45 ms | 14 / 0.45 ms |
| 500 queued 100 KB messages: Redis CPU | 0.35 ms | 0.69 ms | 0.67 ms |
| No messages: commands per second, 1 queue / 3 queues | 1.4 / 1.4 | 5.9 / 13.1 | 5.9 / 13.1 |

The put back runs only when a reply arrives without credit. The usual path costs what it did at `d2eb6f6`, with a pop reply 4 bytes longer, for the list it came from.

</details>

<details>
<summary>What this keeps, and the test that checks it</summary>

The tests are in `t/integration/test_redis_unacked.py` unless noted, with and without `global_keyprefix`.

- Each message stays in exactly one place. A Hypothesis state machine publishes (with and without a token, to several queues and priorities), polls, times out pops, kills consumers (also right after they read a message), acks, rejects and requeues. It also takes a consumer's credit away and gives it back, and lets the visibility timeout pass before `restore_visible` runs, both also while a reply is pending or paused. After every step it checks that each message is in a queue list, in `unacked`, or acked, and in only one of them, and that no message is delivered twice unless the consumer that had it was lost or it was requeued. It also checks that `unacked` and its index list the same tags, that a consumer never has more unacked messages than its prefetch or gets more than one message per pop, and that `no_ack` messages are delivered once and never recorded. On main it fails after two steps: a pop sent, then a publish.
- The record matches `QoS.append`, byte for byte. A Hypothesis property runs the script on generated messages: kombu's layout and others, header keys and values such as `delivery_tag` or `"properties": {`, quotes, backslashes, non-ASCII text, and bytes that aren't JSON. Main and this branch also restored and acked each other's records, in both directions.
- A consumer killed right after a pop keeps the message, whether it was queued or published while the consumer waited, through `drain_events()` and through the event loop. An idle consumer then restores it once the visibility timeout passes. Fails on main.
- An event loop callback reads one reply at most (unit test), and `drain_events()` keeps waiting for the reply to the command a handler sent (unit test). The state machine also uses `basic_get` and polls with a tag the script read differently, and checks that no consumer keeps any per-message state.
- A consumer process paused with `SIGSTOP` while it waits, then killed while a message is published, leaves the message in its queue. Fails on main, where `BRPOP` already took it.
- A full `noeviction` server keeps the message (main raises `OutOfMemoryError` and loses it), and `SCRIPT FLUSH` doesn't stop a consumer. These change the whole server, so they skip under pytest-xdist.
- An idle consumer gets a message from this version's publisher in under a second, and one from an older publisher once its wait times out. With a 10 s wait, three idle consumers share a burst of 30 messages within 3 s. An idle consumer sends a pop and a wait per `brpop_timeout`, also with a leftover token.
- No keys are left after a queue is deleted or expires, and the delivery order (priority, first in first out, alternating queues, requeue) is the same as main. Both pass on main too.
- Unit tests (`t/unit/transport/test_redis.py`) pin the consumer's states and the publish commands. Each fails on main or when one line of the change is removed or altered.
- The paused-reply tests in `test_redis_brpop_qos.py` now pause a wait whose token arrives (its message is still queued) or that times out. A script reply that arrives without credit is put back instead, in the event loop and in `drain_events()`. In another integration test, a recorded reply arrives without credit and `restore_visible` runs past the timeout; once the credit is back, the message is delivered once. It fails without the put back.

All Redis integration tests pass on Redis 7.4.12, Redis 6.2.24 and Valkey 8.1.11, and the unit suite fails only where main fails here. By hand, a Sentinel failover kept a recorded message, and the consumer went on with the new master.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Interleavings</summary>

- The script ran but its reply was lost, as when the connection drops. The message is in `unacked`, and `restore_visible` puts it back once the visibility timeout passes. It's delayed, not lost.
- A pop reply arrives after the consumer lost its credit, because its prefetch limit was reached or lowered while the pop was pending. The consumer puts the message back at the end of the list it was popped from, so it's popped next, and drops its record, in one script. If `restore_visible` already put it back, the script does nothing, so the message isn't queued twice. A message popped again records the same tag. The script tells the records apart by their score in the index, the time of the pop. A reply read later than the visibility timeout after its pop was sent is put back the same way. Pausing such a reply instead would let a restore requeue it in the meantime, and the message would be delivered twice.
- A task that runs longer than the visibility timeout is restored and runs again, as on main. Delivery stays at least once.
- Wake tokens can race. A woken consumer may find the queue empty when another consumer took the message first. Messages published together leave one token, which the script passes on while messages are left. These cost latency, not messages, since a consumer pops anyway once its wait times out, after up to `brpop_timeout`. A wait paused because its consumer has no credit can take a queue's only token, and another idle consumer then gets that message after up to `brpop_timeout`.
- When the script recorded a message under another tag than its own, the QoS writes the message's record and drops the script's one in one `MULTI`/`EXEC`.
- A very large message holds Redis longer while the script copies it into Lua and back, about 1.4 µs per KB, and the record copies it again. Other clients wait meanwhile, as they do for any script.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Choices I made</summary>

- No transport option to turn this off. A mix of publishers only delays messages from older ones, by up to `brpop_timeout`. An opt-out would keep a `BRPOP` path that loses messages on a kill.
- `RPOP` comes first in the script. A full `noeviction` server allows it, and once a script has written, Redis lets its later writes through.
- kombu writes `properties` last. The script decodes only that part: from the last `"properties": {` in the final 2 KB to the message's last brace, which decodes only when it's the top-level key. Other layouts get a full decode. A message that isn't kombu JSON, or whose tag, exchange or routing key isn't printable ASCII, comes back unrecorded, and the QoS records it as on main.
- An event loop callback no longer blocks on a Redis reply. It sends the next command and returns, and a later callback reads the reply when the socket is readable. `drain_events()` waits for that reply within its timeout, so it doesn't sleep `polling_interval` in between.
- The consumer compares the tag the script recorded with the message's own. They match in practice. On a mismatch it logs a warning, and the QoS records the message under its own tag, as on main, in the `MULTI`/`EXEC` that drops the script's record.
- A pop reply that arrives after the consumer lost its credit is put back, not delivered or paused. The poller still pauses a `BLPOP` wait, as #2776 does for `BRPOP`, since a wait moves no message.
- When a pop leaves messages behind, the script puts a token back for a second idle consumer. When it leaves every queue empty, it tells the consumer, which then waits instead of popping again.
- A publish uses a transaction only when it also sets the queue's expiry, as on main.
- A queue deleted while it has no bindings keeps its wake list, as it keeps its lists on main. A consumer on main leaves the last token in place, one key per queue.
- Large messages cost Redis more CPU than on main, because Redis copies a message into Lua and back at about 1.4 µs per KB.

</details>
